title: Given ropes of different lengths, connecting two ropes costs the sum of their lengths, and the combined rope can be connected again. Find the minimum total cost to connect all ropes into one. Explain why always joining the two shortest ropes is optimal and how a min-heap implements it.
shortTitle: Connect Ropes (Minimum Cost to Connect All Ropes)

s1_definition.profdef: Connect Ropes is a Top K Elements problem with a greedy min-heap. Because every join costs the sum of the two joined lengths and that sum is then re-joined later, shorter ropes should be combined first so their lengths are counted in fewer future sums. We repeatedly extract the two smallest lengths from a min-heap, add them, accumulate that cost, and push the combined length back, until one rope remains.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, we merge many small daily settlement batches into one, and merging two batches costs effort equal to their combined size, which then gets merged again. To minimise total effort we always merge the two smallest batches first, because their sizes will otherwise be re-counted in every later merge.
s1_definition.oneliner: Always join the two shortest ropes using a min-heap, add each join's cost, and push the result back until one rope remains.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Connect Ropes is a Top K Elements problem with a greedy min-heap. Because every join costs the sum of the two joined lengths and that sum is then re-joined later, shorter ropes should be combined first so their lengths are counted in fewer future sums. We repeatedly extract the two smallest lengths from a min-heap, add them, accumulate that cost, and push the combined length back, until one rope remains.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, we merge many small daily settlement batches into one, and merging two batches costs effort equal to their combined size, which then gets merged again. To minimise total effort we always merge the two smallest batches first, because their sizes will otherwise be re-counted in every later merge.

**One line to remember:** Always join the two shortest ropes using a min-heap, add each join's cost, and push the result back until one rope remains.

sections.s2_technical:
We load all rope lengths into a min-heap so the two smallest are always at hand. While the heap has more than one rope, we poll the two smallest, add them into `cost`, accumulate `cost` into a running total, and offer `cost` back as a new combined rope. For example, `int first = minHeap.poll(); int second = minHeap.poll(); int cost = first + second; total += cost; minHeap.offer(cost);`. When one rope remains, `total` is the minimum cost.

The greedy choice of always joining the two smallest is optimal because of a Huffman-coding argument: a rope joined early participates in more subsequent sums, so the shortest ropes, which contribute the least, should be joined earliest to be re-summed the most, and the longest ropes should be joined last to be re-summed the fewest times. This minimises the weighted total.

A senior nuance is that this is structurally identical to building a Huffman tree, where the total cost equals the sum over all leaves of length times depth, and the min-heap is the standard way to always pick the two lightest nodes. Loading the heap is O(n), and each of the n minus one joins is O(log n). Complexity is O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India merges many small settlement batches into one final batch, where merging two batches costs effort proportional to their combined size and the merged batch is merged again. Operations want the minimum total effort. This is exactly how Connect Ropes works.

Problem 2 — Merging in an arbitrary order wastes effort because large early merges get re-counted. This is why we always merge the two smallest batches first using a min-heap, which is provably optimal.

The code defines a `BatchMergeService` exposing `minMergeCost(sizes)` returning the minimum total cost. A `Demo` merges a set of batch sizes and logs the minimum cost.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: batch sizes 1, 3, 11, 5.

Step 1: Load the min-heap; the two smallest are 1 and 3. Merge them for cost 4; total is 4. Push 4 back; the heap holds 4, 5, 11.

Step 2: The two smallest are now 4 and 5. Merge them for cost 9; total is 4 plus 9 equals 13. Push 9 back; the heap holds 9, 11.

Step 3: The two smallest are 9 and 11. Merge them for cost 20; total is 13 plus 20 equals 33. Push 20 back; the heap holds only 20.

Step 4: One rope remains, so the minimum total cost is 33.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Connect Ropes is a greedy Top K Elements problem. Joining two ropes costs the sum of their lengths, and because the combined rope is joined again later, every length gets re-counted in all the merges it participates in. The optimal strategy is therefore to always join the two shortest ropes first, so that the smallest lengths, which cost the least, are the ones re-summed the most times, while the largest lengths are joined last and re-summed the fewest times.

I implement this with a min-heap of all the lengths. While more than one rope remains, I poll the two smallest, add them to get the cost of that join, accumulate that cost into a running total, and push the combined length back into the heap so it can be joined again. When a single rope is left, the accumulated total is the minimum cost. This is structurally the same as building a Huffman tree, where the total equals the sum of each leaf's length times its depth.

At the National Bank of India I used this when merging many small settlement batches into one final batch, where each merge costs effort proportional to the combined size and the merged batch is merged again. I always merged the two smallest batches first using a min-heap, which minimised total effort, running in n log n time. Explaining the greedy exchange argument, that the shortest ropes should be re-summed the most, and the Huffman connection is what shows an interviewer I understand why the greedy choice is provably optimal.
